quote: Problem: Ein beliebiges Continuum auf das Innere des Kreises abzu- bilden
english: Problem: to map an arbitrary continuum onto the interior of the circle.
topic: The page completes a remark on determining number fields with Hilbert's own methods, states the problem of mapping an arbitrary continuum onto the interior of a circle and gives a geometric reformulation, and reflects on the importance of number theory and geometric intuition for mathematicians.

triage.modern_statement: Most likely this is the Riemann mapping problem. Read 'Continuum' in the 19th-century sense of a planar region (Gebiet), and 'abbilden' as a conformal map. The question is then: given any simply connected open set G in the complex plane, other than the whole plane, prove that there is a bijective holomorphic (conformal) map from G onto the open unit disk. Riemann stated this in 1851, but his proof relied on the Dirichlet principle and was not rigorous. A second reading is possible: a purely topological (homeomorphic) map onto the disk. The diary snippet alone doesn't settle which one Hilbert meant.
triage.answered_by: W. F. Osgood gave the first correct proof of the general Riemann mapping theorem in 1900. H. A. Schwarz had earlier proved special cases, for example convex regions with suitable boundaries. Hilbert himself rescued the Dirichlet principle in 1900, which restored Riemann's own method. Koebe and Poincaré proved the general uniformization theorem in 1907, which settles Hilbert's 22nd problem in the one-dimensional case. Koebe and Carathéodory later gave further proofs.

evidence.claim: Osgood was the first to give a correct proof of the Riemann mapping theorem, which says every simply connected domain (other than C) can be mapped conformally onto the unit disk.
Riemann's proof was flawed because it depended on the Dirichlet principle. The theorem says every non-empty simply connected open proper subset of C is biholomorphic to the unit disk.
Riemann stated the theorem in his 1851 dissertation. Weierstrass pointed out that the proof was insufficient. Schwarz gave correct proofs for special regions.
Fifty years after Riemann, Hilbert succeeded in proving the Dirichlet principle (1900), which established Riemann's existence theorems.
Hilbert's 22nd problem (uniformization) was solved in dimension one by Poincaré and Koebe in 1907.

triage.why: The wording 'map an arbitrary continuum onto the interior of the circle' fits the classical Riemann mapping problem as it was posed before 1900, when 'Continuum' was used for a connected region. This was a live issue in the 1890s because Riemann's Dirichlet-principle proof had been discredited. Hilbert worked on exactly this: his 1900 rescue of the Dirichlet principle, and his 22nd problem on uniformization. The problem itself isn't one of the 23 problems as stated, but it's a special case of the uniformization theme behind Problem 22. It was solved by Osgood in 1900 and more generally by Koebe and Poincaré in 1907, so it is no longer open. Some research around it is still active (for example, computing conformal maps and their boundary behaviour), but the existence question is settled. Confidence is medium rather than high for two reasons. Matching this diary line to the Riemann mapping problem is my interpretation; no source discusses this note directly. And the alternative topological reading can't be ruled out from the snippet.
